extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and creative writers interested in narrative theory and narratology
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic and prescriptive principles for creating and reading narrative fiction, with emphasis on embedded texts, narrator status, temporality, sequential ordering, and focalization. Useful for writers shaping story effects and for critics/students analyzing narrative technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of suspense: reader-knows vs character-knows
rubrics_metrics.description: From the kind in which both reader and character are equally in the dark, we have stepped up to a second kind: the reader knows, but the character does not, how the fabula will end. The question the reader raises is not 'How does it end?' but 'Will the character discover it in time?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disparity between reader knowledge and character knowledge to create suspense that hinges on discovery rather than outcome; maintain uncertainty because resemblance between embedded and primary fabula is never perfect. Example: suspense persists until the character might or might not interpret signs in time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror-text placement and function
rubrics_metrics.description: When a mirror-text has been added more towards the end of the primary text, suspense presents itself less emphatically... Its function is mostly to enhance or inflect significance. The paraphrase of the primary and of the embedded text... will have a more general meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing mirror-texts early makes them predictive; placing them late makes them retrospective and thematic (e.g., general moral or leitmotif). Avoid mere repetition of the primary fabula as mirror-text; instead aim to enhance, inflect, or lift narration to another level of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded text as a sign/directive for reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The mirror-text serves as directions for use: the embedded story contains a suggestion of how the text should be read... the embedded text functions as a sign to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design embedded passages to signal interpretive frames (irony, foreshadowing, parable). These embedded signs can shape reader expectations and the reading stance toward the primary narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded text interpreted by the actor (an indication to the actor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor her- or himself may also interpret the mirror-text as a sign. In this way she may discern the course of the fabula in which she is herself engaged. Thus the actor can influence the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make embedded texts legible to characters when you want them to act upon them; double meanings in embedded passages can enable characters to reinterpret their situation (example Poe's 'Fall of the House of Usher'). Consider dramatic consequences when characters correctly or incorrectly interpret embedded signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning as poetics (literature requires doubleness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The embedded text, with its double meaning, consists of a piece of literature. This text, interpreted in the widest sense, suggests: 'Literature has (at least) a double meaning, or it is not literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed multiplicity of meaning (puns, double readings) to indicate a poetics; use titles and wordplay to foreshadow multiplicity. Avoid purely single-layered embedded texts if you intend literary depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and function of non-narrative embedded texts
rubrics_metrics.description: By far the majority of embedded texts are non-narrative. No story is related in them. The content of an embedded text may be anything... The predominant form is dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embedded non-narrative passages (dialogue, description, confidences) to diversify texture and to introduce dramatic or expository material without creating a full secondary fabula. Recognize that embedded dialogue is dramatic in kind and can shift tone and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue increases dramatic quality but presentation matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The more dialogue a narrative text contains, the more dramatic that text is... since not only quantity matters here. Also, how the dialogues are presented influences the degree to which a text may be experienced as dramatic. When between each utterance of an actor the primary narrator intervenes... the hierarchical relationship between N1 and N2 remains clearly visible. When the clauses follow each other without intervention by the N1, we are likely to forget that we are dealing with an embedded dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To heighten dramatic immediacy, present dialogue with minimal intervening narration; to preserve narrative hierarchy or commentary, intersperse narrator tags and commentary. Be deliberate about narrator intrusion to control reader awareness of narrative levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded monologue/soliloquy as flexible device
rubrics_metrics.description: When the embedded text is spoken – or thought – by one actor, it is a soliloquy or monologue. The content of a monologue can, again, be practically anything. There is no intrinsic difference between an embedded monologue and other language use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monologues for interiority and to provide confidences, reflections, or description; treat them as rhetorically equivalent to other embedded speech but exploit the single-voice intimacy for subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: All narratives imply a speaker and an interlocutor
rubrics_metrics.description: All utterances, and hence all narratives, imply a speaker... all speakers address an interlocutor; that 'I' can only be 'I' if there is a 'you' who allows it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design narrative address with awareness of implied audience(s): primary narratee(s) and secondary interlocutors (e.g., Sheherazade's multiple addressees). The presence and nature of narratees shape rhetorical strategies and durability of suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between embedded and primary text is variable
rubrics_metrics.description: The contents of the embedded text sometimes link with those of the primary text; sometimes the embedded is even the primary's natural sequel. At other times the embedded text is completely divorced from the primary text; or has an explanatory function; or is similar to the primary text; or contradicts or contravenes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly choose the relationship type (link, sequel, divorced, explanatory, similar, contradictory) to achieve desired effects (irony, amplification, clarification, dissonance). Do not assume assertions at one level automatically determine whole-text meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratorial distance from the author (avoid conflation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When I speak of the narrator, I do not mean the 'implied author'... The notion of the narrator needs further positioning... the commodified author is as fictitious as any character in a narrative and must be subjected to analytical criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating narrator voice with authorial intention; treat narrator as an agent within the text. Be cautious when inferring biographical or market-driven 'author' stances from narrative voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of narrator as the uttering agent
rubrics_metrics.description: I will rigorously stick to the definition of narrator as 'that agent which utters the (linguistic or other) signs that constitute the text.' Only when we confine ourselves to that definition can we avoid confusions that ultimately lead to an appropriation of authority...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or analysing narratives, identify the narrator pragmatically as the source of utterance (linguistic signs) and map their level, reliability, and limitations accordingly. This prevents wrongful attribution of omniscience or authorial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / focalization as principal tool of subjectification
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary means of manipulation is what is traditionally known as point of view or 'perspective.' The view from which the elements of the fabula are being presented is often of decisive importance for the meaning the reader will assign to the fabula. Focalization... is the principal tool for subjectifying the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose focalizers deliberately to shape sympathy, knowledge, and interpretation. Focalization can be placed 'in or with' agents to create interiority, distance, or irony; it is central to how the fabula is perceived and judged by readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story aspects result from manipulation of fabula and medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects that distinguish the structured story from... the text, and... the fabula... If one regards the text primarily as the product of the use of a medium, and the fabula primarily as the product of the imagination, the story could be regarded as the result of an ordering; as orientated, focused, fleshed out; in short, as subjectivized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand storycraft as operations on material: ordering events, shaping characters, and arranging space/relations. These manipulations determine reception; assess choices by their effects on reader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporality: treat time as thick and multifaceted
rubrics_metrics.description: Time is thick and complex, not at all linear and single-stranded... The time that regulates our lives... is so incorporated... The time of telling, the time of the events, and the suspense of time wherein these two do not match up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit multiple temporal registers (micro time, monumental time, presentism, time of telling vs event-time) to produce psychological effects (alienation, urgency, stagnation). Example: Sheherazade 'steals time' by seducing the king into a different temporality via storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential ordering / anachrony as a deliberate device
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between the arrangement in the story and the chronology of the fabula are called chronological deviations or anachronies... Deviations in sequential ordering may contribute to intense reading... Playing with sequential ordering is... a means of drawing attention to certain things, to emphasize, to bring about aesthetic or psychological effects, to produce suspense...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anachrony (deviations from chronological order) to focus attention, create density, complicate causality, produce suspense, or represent differing interpretations of events. Match complexity of anachrony to reader expectations to avoid gratuitous confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three analytic dimensions of anachrony: direction, distance, and range
rubrics_metrics.description: I give examples of three aspects of chronological deviation: direction, distance, and range. Seen from that moment in the fabula that is being presented when the anachrony intervenes, the event presented in the anachrony lies either in the past or in the future. For the first category I use the term retroversion; for the second, anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning non-chronological ordering, specify: direction (retroversion vs anticipation), how far removed (distance), and how much of the narrative is affected (range). Use these to control clarity and effect; prefer specific labeling over vague 'flashback/flashforward.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of grammatical signals to indicate sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The tenses of the verbs in the text indicate the sequence of events: simple past for the later event; past perfect for the preceding events. But even without such indications in the text there is information that... we can combine... to infer chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ tense and aspect deliberately to cue readers about ordering; if withholding tense cues, provide other contextual markers so readers can infer chronology without undue effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions vs intricate deviations (reader effort and expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If deviations in sequential ordering correspond with conventions, they will not stand out. They can, however, be so intricate as to exact the greatest exertions in following the story... the very effort forces one to reflect also on other elements and aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of reader expectations; conventional devices (e.g., in medias res) are easier to process. Use highly intricate ordering only when you want to force reflection or produce dense simultaneity; otherwise risk losing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation of present and past to convey trauma or fractured self
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement back and forth from present to past to present is the story's basic rhythm... These delicate alternations contribute to the story in a very meaningful way: they provide insight into the broken sense of self... and make the reader experience it with her on an emotional level as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternation between present experience and past memory to model trauma, fractured identity, or recovering memory. Pace alternations to mirror psychological states and to build empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering can function rhetorically (summary, cause-effect, thematic framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of the Iliad... indicates the grudge of Achilles... we are, already at the beginning, presented with a summary of the book's contents: the summary that the muse is asked to sing is what the reader will hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordering strategically (e.g., opening with summary, presenting causes after effects) to frame themes, compress explanation, or foreground fate/causality. Understand rhetorical consequences of presenting events out of chronological causation.
